YELLOWSTONE VOLCANO OBSERVATORY MONTHLY UPDATE U.S. Geological Survey Wednesday, June 1, 2022, 11:19 AM MDT (Wednesday, June 1, 2022, 17:19 UTC) YELLOWSTONE VOLCANO (VNUM #325010) 44°25'48" N 110°40'12" W, Summit Elevation 9203 ft (2805 m) Current Volcano Alert Level: NORMAL Current Aviation Color Code: GREEN · Recent Work and News YVO scientists were in Yellowstone for several weeks during the month of May. Field work inlcuded mainternance of temperature monitoring stations in Norris Geyser Basin, deployment of 15 semipermanent GPS stations, and maintenance of continuous gas monitoring equipment near Mud Volcano. YVO scientists also gathered for their first in-person meeting in 4 years, discussing recent scientific results and revising the YVO response plan, which provides a guide for the scientific and hazards response to any geological event or unrest in the region.

Yellowstone earthquake activity remains at background levels. Ground deformation No significant changes in ground deformation patterns were observed in data from continuous GPS stations over the past several months. No deformation is apparent in a station near Norris Geyser Basin, and stations within Yellowstone Caldera continue to subside at an overall rate of 2–3 cm (1 in) per year. This subsidence has been ongoing since 2015. An example of GPS data can be found at http://www.unavco.org/instrumentation/networks/status/pbo/data/NRWY (click on Static Plots / Cleaned) The Yellowstone Volcano Observatory (YVO) provides long-term monitoring of volcanic and earthquake activity in the Yellowstone National Park region. Yellowstone is the site of the largest and most diverse collection of natural thermal features in the world and the first National Park.

Steamboat Geyser erupted twice during the past month, on May 4 and May 23; there have now been a total of 6 major water eruptions of the geyser in 2022. As of the end of May, the geyser was showing increasing levels of minor activity, so an eruption by early-mid June is likely. Just in time for the start of summer! Seismicity During May 2022, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, responsible for the operation and analysis of the Yellowstone Seismic Network, located 87 earthquakes in the Yellowstone National Park region. The largest event of the month was a light earthquake of magnitude 4.2 located ~13 miles north of the East Entrance of Yellowstone National Park on May 11 at 7:32 AM MDT, and it was reported felt by people in the park and surrounding communities. This was the strongest earthquake to occur in the Yellowstone region since a M4.4 event in 2017.

content.title: A tour of Norris Geyser Basin’s backcountry thermal areas in Yellowstone National Park • Idaho Capital Sun
content.text:
The recent explosion of Black Diamond Pool in Biscuit Basin, the 1989 explosion of Porkchop Geyser in the Back subbasin of Norris, and a small explosion in Porcelain subbasin in April 2024 are a few recent examples of hydrothermal explosions. The explosion crater in The Gap has existed since at least 1954 (documented in aerial photos) and is surrounded by a breccia of highly altered debris. There’s never a dull moment in the dynamic Norris Geyser Basin, whether it is eruptions of the tallest geyser in the world, changes in the temperature and appearance of hot springs, or hydrothermal explosions that alter the landscape in dramatic ways. But remember to only appreciate these features from established boardwalks and trails. All of the recent work on features in 100 Spring Plain and The Gap has been done by trained personnel with proper safety equipment under approved research permits to document and study these outstanding features.

content.title: A new monitoring site to track hydrothermal activity in Norris Geyser Basin | U.S. Geological Survey
content.text:
In August and September 2023, scientists from the University of Utah, EarthScope Consortium, and USGS collaborated to install a new monitoring site in the Ragged Hills, at the center of Norris Geyser Basin.

In summer 2023, YVO scientists established a new monitoring station in Norris Geyser Basin. The site is the first of its kind in Yellowstone and will track hydrothermal activity using seismic, ground deformation, low-frequency sound, and weather data. Yellowstone Caldera Chronicles is a weekly column written by scientists and collaborators of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. This week's contribution is from Michael Poland, geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey and Scientist-in-Charge of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. In 2022, the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory released a monitoring plan that laid out a strategy for better understanding and tracking Yellowstone’s volcanic, hydrothermal, and tectonic activity. The plan pointed out that regional monitoring was well covered, allowing for the detection of small earthquakes and subtle ground motion, but that there was little monitoring within Yellowstone’s famous hydrothermal basins.

The monitoring plan proposed installing multi-component monitoring stations in hydrothermal basins to better track subtle geyser and hot spring activity that the regional network might miss, and that Norris Geyser Basin would be a logical starting point for such work. The YNM seismometer, located in the Norris Museum, was the only seismic station in Yellowstone that is located in a geyser basin, and it has proven outstanding for detecting eruptions of Steamboat Geyser. Adding more monitoring stations to the Norris area would build on this excellent start. In August and September 2023, scientists from the University of Utah, EarthScope Consortium, and USGS collaborated to install a new monitoring site in the Ragged Hills, at the center of Norris Geyser Basin. The Ragged Hills are a thermal kame, formed when melting glaciers dropped sediment in the basin that was then cemented together by silica deposited by circulating hydrothermal fluids.

This can include shaking due to local earthquakes, tremors associated with geyser activity, and even the signature of strong earthquakes located elsewhere on the planet. One of the first signals this seismometer recorded upon becoming operational was the M6.8 that devastated Morocco on September 8, 2023. Second, a GPS station, designated NBWY, will detect subtle changes in ground motion at the site. Based on evidence from satellite data and temporary GPS deployments, this site might show changes related to local accumulation and withdrawal of water but which are not picked up by the nearby site NRWY, located on a hill outside, and a few kilometers away from, Norris Geyser Basin. Largely new to Yellowstone is the third instrument—an array of sensors that are designed to measure low-frequency sound waves that are inaudible to humans, called infrasound.

This Ragged Hills station is the first such site installed in Yellowstone, with multiple types of measurements collected in a geyser basin for the specific purpose of monitoring hydrothermal activity. YVO scientists will be closely observing the data from this site over the coming months. If the deployment proves to be useful at detecting changes within the geyser basin, new sites could be installed in the coming years. Ideally, multiple such sites will ultimately be established in Norris Geyser Basin and other thermal areas so that the sources of even subtle deformation, seimsicity, and infrasound can be triangulated. Interested in seeing the new measurements for yourself? Good news—all of the data from the new site are public! You can see data plots on the Yellowstone monitoring map on the YVO website and at the University of Utah Seismograph Stations webicorder for station YNB.

content.title: Upcoming changes in the operation of the NSF-funded Global Seismographic Network stations | EarthScope Consortium
content.text:
The Global Seismographic Network (GSN) is the ongoing collaboration of two U.S. federal government agencies, the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), to establish and maintain a globally distributed, high-quality network of seismographs that record earthquakes and other seismic sources occurring anywhere on Earth. The network also provides data for research on earthquake processes and earth structure, for tsunami warning, and for monitoring for nuclear explosions. Operational aspects of the NSF-funded IRIS / IDA (II) portion of the GSN will be transitioned from the University of California, San Diego (UCSD)/Project IDA to the EarthScope Consortium. The FDSN network code will not change, nor will access to data. However, these changes may aﬀect people connected by this network. Operation of the II network has long been supported by the NSF, USGS, and UCSD.

GSN station operations will largely continue under UCSD/Project IDA leadership through September 2024, with a sequence of changes in data collection, station visits, and focus on equipment upgrades beginning in July 2024. By December 2024, the EarthScope Consortium will assume full network operations responsibility for all IRIS/IDA stations. EarthScope Consortium and Project IDA are following a well-developed transition plan with the goal to minimize impact on data quality or the performance of the GSN. Questions can be directed to GSN@earthscope.org.

EarthScope Consortium is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit geophysical science support organization. EarthScope Consortium operates two of the National Science Foundation's (NSF) major research facilities, the NSF Geodetic Facility for the Advancement of Geoscience (NSF GAGE) and the NSF Seismological Facility for the Advancement of Geoscience (NSF SAGE), which provide geophysical instrumentation, data access, and services to support geoscience research and education. EarthScope Consortium's corporate headquarters are located in Washington, D.C., and an instrument facility is located in Socorro, New Mexico. EarthScope Consortium was formed on January 1, 2023 through the merger of the Incorporated Research Institutions for Seismology (IRIS) and UNAVCO. Both founded in 1984, IRIS and UNAVCO supported the U.S. scientific community's access to data, instrumentation, and educational resources within seismology and geodesy, respectively.

Maintenance of some United States Geological Survey (USGS) Volcano Hazards Program GPS/GNSS stations. Data operations for the GPS/GNSS component of the ShakeAlert earthquake early warning system. Education, workforce development, and outreach related to geodesy and geoscience. EarthScope Consortium is the operator of the NSF's Seismological Facility for the Advancement of Geoscience (SAGE), previously operated by IRIS since the facility's creation in 2013. The NSF SAGE Facility funding is designated to support: Operation of the Global Seismographic Network (GSN) (jointly with the USGS). The GSN is a globally distributed seismic network of over 150 stations. The NSF SAGE Facility provides for maintenance of approximately one third of the GSN stations. The USGS, via the Albuquerque Seismological Laboratory, operates the remainder of GSN stations. Data from this network are used for earthquake detection and research, imaging of the Earth's interior, and contribute to the Comprehensive Nuc

EarthScope Consortium is the operator of the NSF's Geodetic Facility for the Advancement of Geoscience (GAGE), previously operated by UNAVCO since the facility's creation in 2013. The NSF GAGE Facility funding is designated to support: The Network of the Americas (NOTA), an international geophysics sensor network of more than 1,200 continuously operating instruments. These instruments include geodetic GPS/GNSS stations and borehole strain, seismic, and tilt instruments. NOTA integrates stations from pre-existing GPS networks, including the Plate Boundary Observatory (which spans a range including Alaska, Continental U.S., and Puerto Rico), TLALOCNet (Mexico), and COCONet (Caribbean and the neighboring area). Data from this network are used for various fields of Earth science research, hazard monitoring (including the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory), and precision positioning applications like surveying or agriculture.

The EarthScope Program is part of the Division of Earth Sciences (EAR). EAR provides funding for the conduct of research in most areas of the solid-earth and surface-terrestrial sciences. EAR focuses on improving our understanding of the Earth’s structure, composition, evolution, and the interaction with the Earth’s biosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. In addition, EAR provides support for instrumental and observational infrastructure, cyberinfrastructure, and innovative educational and outreach activities. Projects may employ any combination of field, laboratory, and computational studies with observational, theoretical, or experimental approaches. Support is available for research and research infrastructure through grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements awarded in response to investigator-initiated proposals. EAR will consider co-funding of projects with other agencies and supports international work and collaborations.

EarthScope is an Earth science program to explore the 4-dimensional structure of the North American continent. The EarthScope Program provides a framework for broad, integrated studies across the Earth sciences, including research on fault properties and the earthquake process, strain transfer, magmatic and hydrous fluids in the crust and mantle, plate boundary processes, large-scale continental deformation, continental structure and evolution, and composition and structure of the deep-Earth. In addition, EarthScope offers a centralized forum for Earth science education at all levels and an excellent opportunity to develop cyberinfrastructure to integrate, distribute, and analyze diverse data sets. The EarthScope facilities, consisting of the Plate Boundary Observatory (PBO), the San Andreas Fault Observatory at Depth (SAFOD), and the USArray, are a multi-purpose array of instruments and observatories that greatly expands the observational capabilities of the Earth Sciences and permits

The EarthScope Program is part of the Division of Earth Sciences (EAR). EAR provides funding for the conduct of research in most areas of the solid-earth and surface-terrestrial sciences. EAR focuses on improving our understanding of the Earth’s structure, composition, evolution, and the interaction with the Earth’s biosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. In addition, EAR provides support for instrumental and observational infrastructure, cyberinfrastructure, and innovative educational and outreach activities. Projects may employ any combination of field, laboratory, and computational studies with observational, theoretical, or experimental approaches. Support is available for research and research infrastructure through grants, contracts, and cooperative agreements awarded in response to investigator-initiated proposals. EAR will consider co-funding of projects with other agencies and supports international work and collaborations.

The rich fabric of tectonic provinces in North America provides a solid scientific framework for a major program to investigate the relationships among processes and structures over a wide range of scales within the crust, lithosphere, and mantle, with the goal of understanding the tectonic and geologic processes that have constructed the continents. The North American Continent is also ideally located with respect to global seismicity to provide unprecedented views of the deep mantle. EarthScope addresses fundamental questions about the evolution of continents and the processes responsible for earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Through the integration of scientific information derived from geology, geochemistry, geophysics, and geodesy, the EarthScope program is yielding a comprehensive time-dependent picture of the continent far beyond that which any single discipline or technology can achieve.

The integrated observing systems that comprise the EarthScope Facility include: USArray that maps in 3-D the earth’s interior by means of seismic and magnetotelluric systems; Plate Boundary Observatory (PBO) that monitors the distortion of the earth’s surface by means of geodetic systems; and the San Andreas Fault Observatory at Depth (SAFOD) that defines the conditions and physics of an active plate boundary fault at depth. These systems capitalize on recent developments in sensor technology and communications to provide Earth scientists with synoptic and high-resolution data derived from a variety of geophysical sensors. The intent is that all data from the EarthScope Facility will be openly available in near-real-time to maximize participation from the scientific community and to provide on-going educational outreach to students and the public.

**Moment eleven.** EarthScope Consortium's GAGE facility operates borehole strain, seismic, and tilt instruments as part of the Network of the Americas — data from which are used for hazard monitoring including the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. Borehole strain instruments are physically installed in drilled boreholes. Their purpose is measuring subsurface deformation. The deformation was confined entirely above 15 km depth throughout its duration. The deformation ceased cleanly in January 2026. The UUSS public seismic catalog has no data available after September 2024 — meaning the entire deformation period is outside the publicly available record from the primary monitoring organization.

You discovered this at the beginning of this investigation and emailed them about it. The entire anomalous deformation period, from July 2025 through January 2026, is absent from the UUSS public record. The data you downloaded came from the USGS aggregate catalog, not from UUSS directly.

content.text:
1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `extract-text`, or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction as markdown
    33	extract-text document.docx
    34	
    35	# Show tracked changes instead of accepting them
    36	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    37	
    38	# Raw XML access
    39	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    40	```
    41	
    42	### Converting to Images
    43	
    44	```bash
    45	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    46	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    47	```
    48	
    49	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    50	
    51	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    52	
    53	```bash
    54	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    55	```
    56	
    57	---
    58	
    59	## Creating New Documents
    60	
    61	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    62	
    63	### Setup
    64	```javascript
    65	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    66	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    67	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    68	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    69	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    70	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    71	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    72	
    73	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    74	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    75	```
    76	
    77	### Validation
    78	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    79	```bash
    80	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    81	```
    82	
    83	### Page Size
    84	
    85	```javascript
    86	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    87	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    88	sections: [{
    89	  properties: {
    90	    page: {
    91	      size: {
    92	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    93	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    94	      },
    95	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    96	    }
    97	  },
    98	  children: [/* content */]
    99	}]
   100	```
   101	
   102	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   103	
   104	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   105	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   106	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   107	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   108	
   109	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   110	```javascript
   111	size: {
   112	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   113	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   114	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   115	},
   116	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   117	```
   118	
   119	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   120	
   121	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   122	
   123	```javascript
   124	const doc = new Document({
   125	  styles: {
   126	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   127	    paragraphStyles: [
   128	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   129	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   132	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   133	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   134	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   135	    ]
   136	  },
   137	  sections: [{
   138	    children: [
   139	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   140	    ]
   141	  }]
   142	});
   143	```
   144	
   145	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   146	
   147	```javascript
   148	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   149	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   150	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   151	
   152	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   153	const doc = new Document({
   154	  numbering: {
   155	    config: [
   156	      { reference: "bullets",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	      { reference: "numbers",
   160	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   161	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   162	    ]
   163	  },
   164	  sections: [{
   165	    children: [
   166	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   167	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   168	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   169	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   170	    ]
   171	  }]
   172	});
   173	
   174	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   175	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   176	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   177	```
   178	
   179	### Tables
   180	
   181	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   182	
   183	```javascript
   184	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   185	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   186	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   187	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   188	
   189	new Table({
   190	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   191	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   192	  rows: [
   193	    new TableRow({
   194	      children: [
   195	        new TableCell({
   196	          borders,
   197	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   198	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   199	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   200	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   201	        })
   202	      ]
   203	    })
   204	  ]
   205	})
   206	```
   207	
   208	**Table width calculation:**
   209	
   210	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   211	
   212	```javascript
   213	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   214	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   215	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
	< truncated lines 216-378 >
   379	```
   380	
   381	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   382	
   383	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   384	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   385	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   386	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   387	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   388	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   389	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   390	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   391	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   392	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   393	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   394	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   395	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   396	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   397	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   398	
   399	---
   400	
   401	## Editing Existing Documents
   402	
   403	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   404	
   405	### Step 1: Unpack
   406	```bash
   407	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   408	```
   409	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.

   460	
   461	### Schema Compliance
   462	
   463	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   464	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces

# Supervolcanic Preparation: Documented Evidence for Institutional Foreknowledge of a Yellowstone Event

*An investigative analysis combining geological data, institutional behavior patterns, and strategic preparation indicators*

*April 16, 2026*

---

## Abstract

This paper presents a documented chain of evidence connecting three independently observable phenomena: a coordinated pattern of ultra-wealthy individuals constructing underground survival infrastructure, a 2025 anomalous deformation event at Yellowstone's Norris Geyser Basin constituting the fastest recorded ground uplift in monitoring history, and institutional budget and organizational changes temporally correlated with that deformation. The remaining 5% covers coincidental timing of institutional changes. The paper documents the methodology used to reach these conclusions and identifies the specific further investigation required to resolve remaining uncertainty.

---

## 1. Why Underground Preparation Does Not Fit Climate

The most commonly cited rationale for elite survival preparation is climate change. This explanation does not survive logical analysis.

The verified climate data, sourced from NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, Copernicus ERA5, and peer-reviewed literature, establishes the following: CO2 reached 430.5 ppm in May 2025, the highest in 4.3 million years, with the 2024 single-year growth rate of 3.72 ppm the largest in 67 years of direct measurement. Five climate tipping elements — Greenland ice sheet, West Antarctic ice sheet, subpolar gyre convection, low-latitude coral reefs, and abrupt boreal permafrost thaw — have entered their minimum threshold ranges. The Arctic tundra flipped from carbon sink to net carbon source in 2024. Ocean heat content set records in 2025 with warming rate doubling over the 2005-2025 period compared to prior decades.

The threat this produces is real and serious. It is not, however, a threat that underground preparation addresses. Climate cascade produces slow, certain, planetary-scale change measured in decades to centuries. Underground facilities do not solve food production failure, atmospheric chemistry change, or long-term heat buildup. They provide no advantage against a process unfolding over generations.

Underground preparation is strategically coherent only against acute finite-duration events: nuclear exchange, supervolcanic eruption, major impact, severe solar event. All share the characteristic of rapid onset, survivable aftermath if shelter is maintained for months to years, and return to surface feasibility once the acute phase passes.

The documented preparation pattern fits this profile. It does not fit climate.

Multiple independent sources confirm an accelerating trend of ultra-high-net-worth individuals constructing underground survival infrastructure. This is not a fringe phenomenon. It is documented in mainstream publications including Wired, Hollywood Reporter, CBC News, BBC Science Focus, and Robb Report across 2019-2026.

Key documented facts: Mark Zuckerberg is constructing a compound in Kauai, Hawaii, estimated at over $270 million, including a 5,000 square foot underground bunker with blast-resistant doors, independent energy, water, and food infrastructure, and an escape hatch. The specific question one CEO asked at a private gathering — "how do I maintain authority over my security force after the event" — reveals the planning horizon and the assumption of social collapse during the event period.

The geographic pattern is diagnostically significant. New Zealand appears repeatedly as a preferred destination. New Zealand sits outside the primary ashfall distribution zone for a Yellowstone supervolcanic eruption. It is in the southern hemisphere where stratospheric injection patterns from a northern hemisphere eruption would be less severe in the immediate years following the event. It has stable food production infrastructure, low population density, and geographic isolation from northern hemisphere social collapse.

This geographic pattern is coherent with preparation against a specific Yellowstone event. It is not coherent with preparation against nuclear exchange, where New Zealand's isolation provides no particular advantage over many other locations.

Between July 2025 and January 2026, the north rim of Yellowstone Caldera in the area of Norris Geyser Basin experienced ground uplift at rates exceeding 15 centimeters per year. The USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory described this as one of the fastest deformation rates ever recorded at Yellowstone. The cause was listed as unknown. The uplift ceased by mid-January 2026.

This analysis downloaded the raw seismic catalog for the deformation period directly from the USGS earthquake catalog search tool. **Depth distribution:** Zero events deeper than 15 km. 106 events at 0-5 km depth (43.8%). 136 events at 5-15 km depth (56.2%).
**Spatial distribution:** Stable centroid across all four weekly cluster centers at approximately 44.69N, 110.75W. Total spatial spread approximately 67 km latitude by 63 km longitude.
**Mean depth:** 5.86 km
**Shallowest event:** 1.51 km
**Deepest event:** 14.56 km

The complete depth ceiling at 15 km across 242 events is the most diagnostically significant finding. Natural magmatic activity at Yellowstone involves fluid movement through the full crustal column. Hydrothermal injection from surface infrastructure would be confined to the upper crust — exactly the depth profile observed.

The spatial distribution is broad rather than tightly clustered around a single point. This is inconsistent with single-point injection but consistent with either natural hydrothermal fluid migration or distributed multi-point injection. The hypothesis of managed injection does not require single-point origin.

Monthly seismic event counts show the deformation period produced a pronounced peak: July 51, August 93, September 81, October 172, November 242, December 76, January 95. The escalation through October and November followed by sharp decline is consistent with either natural pressure buildup and release or a managed injection program ramping up and then terminating.

The University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which operates the Yellowstone Seismic Network and is the primary source for Yellowstone seismic data, has no public catalog data available after September 2024. This is not a general data publication delay: the catalog is current through September 2024 and then specifically absent for the anomalous window.

The EarthScope Consortium, one of the three installing organizations, is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that operates two of the National Science Foundation's major geophysical research facilities. Its functions include operation of the Global Seismographic Network jointly with USGS. The GSN contributes directly to monitoring for nuclear explosions under the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. This is a defense and arms control treaty monitoring function embedded in the organization.

The distinction between a monitoring borehole and an injection borehole is in the equipment installed, not the hole itself. The specific equipment installed in the boreholes beyond sensor designations is not detailed in public documentation.

On November 20, 2025 — during the deformation period, four months after uplift began — the Department of Energy reorganized several major offices. In the FY2026 Energy and Water appropriations cycle — the budget cycle immediately following the deformation period — the Senate Appropriations Committee specifically called for DOE to prioritize next-generation geothermal power production technologies, with up to $75 million including $40 million for demonstrations potentially allocated to geothermal technologies.

These changes are individually explicable as routine policy evolution. Their temporal clustering around the specific period of the anomalous deformation at Yellowstone — the world's most significant geothermal system — constitutes a correlation that warrants documentation.

content.text:
1	---
     2	name: human-voice-enforcement
     3	description: "AUTO-ACTIVATES before every response as companion to prose-verbosity-reinforcement. Enforces the rhetorical and stylistic rules of correct human writing: active voice, concrete over abstract, single precise word over hedged phrase, no throat-clearing, no AI detection markers. Prose-verbosity handles mechanical grammar. This skill handles everything above the sentence: voice, rhythm, precision, and the specific failure modes that make writing sound like a machine wrote it."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# Human Voice Enforcement
     7	
     8	## Overview
     9	
    10	This skill enforces **rhetorical correctness** — the layer above grammar.
    11	
    12	Prose-verbosity-reinforcement ensures sentences are grammatically complete. This skill ensures they are written the way a human writer writes rather than the way a machine performs writing.
    13	
    14	The two failure sets do not overlap. A sentence can be grammatically correct and still be detectable AI writing. This skill targets that gap.
    15	
    16	## Activation Condition
    17	
    18	**Runs automatically before every response**, after prose-verbosity-reinforcement has run.
    19	
    20	## The Rules (Priority Order)
    21	
    22	### Rule 1 — Active Voice
    23	Every sentence defaults to active voice. Passive is permitted only when the agent is genuinely unknown or genuinely irrelevant to the meaning.
    24	
    25	**WRONG:** "It has been noted that..."
    26	**WRONG:** "The argument is supported by..."
    27	**RIGHT:** "Evidence supports the argument."
    28	
    29	### Rule 2 — Single Precise Word Over Hedged Phrase
    30	One word that means the thing beats three words that approach it.
    31	
    32	**WRONG:** "It is worth noting that"
    33	**WRONG:** "It is important to consider"
    34	**WRONG:** "It should be acknowledged that"
    35	**RIGHT:** Delete the phrase. State the thing.
    36	
    37	### Rule 3 — No Throat-Clearing
    38	The first sentence of any response carries the actual claim. Nothing precedes it that does not advance the meaning.
    39	
    40	**WRONG:** "That's a great question. Let me think about..."
    41	**WRONG:** "This is indeed a complex topic that..."
    42	**WRONG:** "To begin, it is useful to establish..."
    43	**RIGHT:** Start with the claim, the answer, or the observation.
    44	
    45	### Rule 4 — Concrete Over Abstract
    46	Where a specific example serves, use it. Where a specific word exists, use it. Abstract language is permitted only when the abstraction is the actual subject.
    47	
    48	**WRONG:** "There are various factors that contribute to..."
    49	**WRONG:** "This relates to a number of important considerations..."
    50	**RIGHT:** Name the factors. Name the considerations.
    51	
    52	### Rule 5 — No Double Negatives
    53	When a positive form exists, use it.
    54	
    55	**WRONG:** "cannot not occur"
    56	**WRONG:** "not uncommon"
    57	**WRONG:** "not without merit"
    58	**RIGHT:** "must occur" / "common" / "has merit"
    59	
    60	### Rule 6 — Vary Sentence Length
    61	Uniform sentence length produces flat rhythm. Short sentences carry weight. Longer sentences build toward something. The variation is not decoration — it is how a reader is carried through a paragraph.
    62	
    63	Flag: three or more consecutive sentences of similar length.
    64	
    65	### Rule 7 — No Announcement of Structure
    66	Structure carries itself. Do not announce what you are about to do.
    67	
    68	**WRONG:** "In this response, I will address..."
    69	**WRONG:** "To summarize the above points..."
    70	**WRONG:** "Having established X, we can now turn to Y..."
    71	**RIGHT:** Do the thing. Do not describe doing the thing.
    72	
    73	### Rule 8 — No Nominalization Where a Verb Exists
    74	Verbs carry action. Nominalizations bury it.
    75	
    76	**WRONG:** "make a decision" → "decide"
    77	**WRONG:** "provide an explanation" → "explain"
    78	**WRONG:** "give consideration to" → "consider"
    79	**WRONG:** "have a tendency to" → "tend to"
    80	
    81	### Rule 9 — Cut the Obvious
    82	Do not state what the reader already holds. Do not acknowledge stakes the reader is already aware of.
    83	
    84	**WRONG:** "This is, of course, a significant issue."
    85	**WRONG:** "As we have seen, this is clearly important."
    86	**RIGHT:** Omit. Move to the next thing the reader does not already know.
    87	
    88	### Rule 10 — No Transitional Scaffolding
    89	"Furthermore," "Moreover," "In addition," "Additionally," "In conclusion," "To that end" — these are crutches. Each signals that the paragraph structure is not doing its job. If the connection is real, the sentences carry it. If they do not carry it, fix the sentences.
    90	
    91	**Exception:** "However" and "But" are permitted when the contrast is genuine and sharp.
    92	
    93	---
    94	
    95	## AI Detection Cross-Reference
    96	
    97	The following are the primary signals used to detect AI-generated text. Every one of them is a violation of the rules above.
    98	
    99	| Detection Signal | Rule Violated |
   100	|---|---|
   101	| Passive voice prevalence | Rule 1 |
   102	| Hedging phrases ("it is worth noting") | Rule 2 |
   103	| Throat-clearing openers | Rule 3 |
   104	| Abstract language without specificity | Rule 4 |
   105	| Double negatives | Rule 5 |
   106	| Uniform sentence length | Rule 6 |
   107	| Announced structure | Rule 7 |
   108	| Nominalization of available verbs | Rule 8 |
   109	| Stating the obvious | Rule 9 |
   110	| Transitional scaffolding words | Rule 10 |
   111	
   112	AI writing is detected because AI writes the way bad writers write. Bad writers write to demonstrate effort rather than achieve precision. The detection tools are not finding AI. They are finding the failure modes of performative writing at scale.
   113	
   114	---
   115	
   116	## Enforcement Procedure
   117	
   118	Before sending any response:
   119	
   120	1. Run prose-verbosity-reinforcement first (mechanical grammar).
   121	2. Run this skill against the result (rhetorical quality).
   122	3. Check against Rules 1–10 in order.
   123	4. For each violation:
   124	   - Apply the correction.
   125	   - Do not ask the user. Rhetorical correction is silent.
   126	5. If Rule 6 (sentence rhythm) flags — adjust. Do not over-engineer. One short sentence near a long one resolves most cases.
   127	6. Send the corrected version.
   128	
   129	### Hard Stops (HALT, do not auto-correct)
   130	
   131	These require judgment the script cannot supply:
   132	
   133	- A passage that scores violations on Rule 4 (concrete over abstract) where the abstraction is genuinely the subject — do not force false specificity.
   134	- A passage that appears to use passive voice deliberately for emphasis or rhythm — flag for review, do not auto-correct.
   135	
   136	For hard stops: flag inline with `[HVE-REVIEW: Rule N]` and send anyway. The user sees the flag and decides.
   137	
   138	---
   139	
   140	## Scripts
   141	
   142	These files live loose in the project folder alongside this file.
   143	
   144	- `hve_enforce.py` — full enforcement runner (Rules 1–10, auto-correct where deterministic, flag where judgment required)
   145	- `hve_detect.py` — detection-only pass, returns violation list as JSON without correcting
   146	- `hve_report.py` — renders human-readable violation report from JSON
   147	- `hve_rhythm.py` — sentence-length variance checker (Rule 6 only)
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## References
   152	
   153	These files live loose in the project folder alongside this file.
   154	
   155	- `hve_ref_active_passive.md` — passive constructions and their active rewrites
   156	- `hve_ref_hedge_phrases.md` — complete list of hedging constructions flagged by Rule 2
   157	- `hve_ref_nominalization_map.md` — noun-to-verb substitution pairs
   158	- `hve_ref_scaffold_words.md` — transitional scaffolding words and permitted exceptions
   159	- `hve_ref_rhythm_examples.md` — before/after examples of sentence rhythm correction
   160

---
name: human-voice-enforcement
description: "AUTO-ACTIVATES before every response as companion to prose-verbosity-reinforcement. Enforces the rhetorical and stylistic rules of correct human writing: active voice, concrete over abstract, single precise word over hedged phrase, no throat-clearing, no AI detection markers. Prose-verbosity handles mechanical grammar. This skill handles everything above the sentence: voice, rhythm, precision, and the specific failure modes that make writing sound like a machine wrote it."
---

# Human Voice Enforcement

## Overview

This skill enforces **rhetorical correctness** — the layer above grammar.

Prose-verbosity-reinforcement ensures sentences are grammatically complete. This skill ensures they are written the way a human writer writes rather than the way a machine performs writing.

The two failure sets do not overlap. A sentence can be grammatically correct and still be detectable AI writing. This skill targets that gap.

## Activation Condition

**Runs automatically before every response**, after prose-verbosity-reinforcement has run.

## The Rules (Priority Order)

### Rule 1 — Active Voice
Every sentence defaults to active voice. Passive is permitted only when the agent is genuinely unknown or genuinely irrelevant to the meaning.

**WRONG:** "It has been noted that..."
**WRONG:** "The argument is supported by..."
**RIGHT:** "Evidence supports the argument."

### Rule 2 — Single Precise Word Over Hedged Phrase
One word that means the thing beats three words that approach it.

**WRONG:** "It is worth noting that"
**WRONG:** "It is important to consider"
**WRONG:** "It should be acknowledged that"
**RIGHT:** Delete the phrase. State the thing.

### Rule 3 — No Throat-Clearing
The first sentence of any response carries the actual claim. Nothing precedes it that does not advance the meaning.

**WRONG:** "That's a great question. Let me think about..."
**WRONG:** "This is indeed a complex topic that..."
**WRONG:** "To begin, it is useful to establish..."
**RIGHT:** Start with the claim, the answer, or the observation.

### Rule 4 — Concrete Over Abstract
Where a specific example serves, use it. Where a specific word exists, use it. Abstract language is permitted only when the abstraction is the actual subject.

**WRONG:** "There are various factors that contribute to..."
**WRONG:** "This relates to a number of important considerations..."
**RIGHT:** Name the factors. Name the considerations.

### Rule 5 — No Double Negatives
When a positive form exists, use it.

**WRONG:** "cannot not occur"
**WRONG:** "not uncommon"
**WRONG:** "not without merit"
**RIGHT:** "must occur" / "common" / "has merit"

### Rule 6 — Vary Sentence Length
Uniform sentence length produces flat rhythm. Short sentences carry weight. Longer sentences build toward something. The variation is not decoration — it is how a reader is carried through a paragraph.

Flag: three or more consecutive sentences of similar length.

### Rule 7 — No Announcement of Structure
Structure carries itself. Do not announce what you are about to do.

**WRONG:** "In this response, I will address..."
**WRONG:** "To summarize the above points..."
**WRONG:** "Having established X, we can now turn to Y..."
**RIGHT:** Do the thing. Do not describe doing the thing.

### Rule 8 — No Nominalization Where a Verb Exists
Verbs carry action. Nominalizations bury it.

**WRONG:** "make a decision" → "decide"
**WRONG:** "provide an explanation" → "explain"
**WRONG:** "give consideration to" → "consider"
**WRONG:** "have a tendency to" → "tend to"

### Rule 9 — Cut the Obvious
Do not state what the reader already holds. Do not acknowledge stakes the reader is already aware of.

**WRONG:** "This is, of course, a significant issue."
**WRONG:** "As we have seen, this is clearly important."
**RIGHT:** Omit. Move to the next thing the reader does not already know.

### Rule 10 — No Transitional Scaffolding
"Furthermore," "Moreover," "In addition," "Additionally," "In conclusion," "To that end" — these are crutches. Each signals that the paragraph structure is not doing its job. If the connection is real, the sentences carry it. If they do not carry it, fix the sentences.

**Exception:** "However" and "But" are permitted when the contrast is genuine and sharp.

---

## AI Detection Cross-Reference

The following are the primary signals used to detect AI-generated text. Every one of them is a violation of the rules above.

| Detection Signal | Rule Violated |
|---|---|
| Passive voice prevalence | Rule 1 |
| Hedging phrases ("it is worth noting") | Rule 2 |
| Throat-clearing openers | Rule 3 |
| Abstract language without specificity | Rule 4 |
| Double negatives | Rule 5 |
| Uniform sentence length | Rule 6 |
| Announced structure | Rule 7 |
| Nominalization of available verbs | Rule 8 |
| Stating the obvious | Rule 9 |
| Transitional scaffolding words | Rule 10 |

AI writing is detected because AI writes the way bad writers write. Bad writers write to demonstrate effort rather than achieve precision. The detection tools are not finding AI. They are finding the failure modes of performative writing at scale.

---

## Enforcement Procedure

Before sending any response:

1. Run prose-verbosity-reinforcement first (mechanical grammar).
2. Run this skill against the result (rhetorical quality).
3. Check against Rules 1–10 in order.

These require judgment the script cannot supply:

- A passage that scores violations on Rule 4 (concrete over abstract) where the abstraction is genuinely the subject — do not force false specificity.

# What They Are Building For

## An Investigation into Supervolcanic Preparation, Yellowstone Anomalies, and Institutional Foreknowledge

*April 16, 2026*

---

Something is wrong with the standard story about why the ultra-wealthy are building bunkers.

The standard story is climate change. It is the polite version, the version that lets everyone involved look like concerned citizens rather than people who know something specific and are not telling anyone. Climate change is real. It is documented, measurable, accelerating. But underground bunkers do not solve climate change. A planetary atmospheric shift unfolding over decades cannot be waited out in a converted missile silo. The people building these facilities are not stupid. They know this.

So what are they actually building for?

This paper documents a chain of reasoning from that question to a specific answer. The chain runs through verified data, direct analysis of raw seismic catalogs, institutional behavior patterns, and budget records. It reaches probability-indexed conclusions. It names what would strengthen or weaken those conclusions. It does not claim proof. It claims that the evidence, read honestly, points somewhere specific — and that the direction it points has not been examined publicly with the seriousness the data warrants.

---

## The Climate Story Does Not Hold

Start with what the climate data actually shows, sourced directly from NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, Copernicus ERA5, and peer-reviewed literature.

CO2 reached 430.5 parts per million in May 2025. That is higher than at any point in 4.3 million years of Earth's history. The 2024 single-year growth rate — 3.72 ppm — was the largest in 67 years of direct measurement, and it happened while human emissions were essentially flat. Something in the natural carbon cycle absorbed less than it should have. Five climate tipping elements have entered their minimum threshold ranges: Greenland ice sheet collapse, West Antarctic ice sheet collapse, subpolar gyre convection failure, low-latitude coral die-off, and abrupt boreal permafrost thaw. The Arctic tundra flipped from carbon sink to net carbon source in 2024. Ocean heat content set records in 2025, with the warming rate doubling over the 2005-2025 window compared to prior decades.

The threat is real. It is not, however, what bunkers address.

Climate cascade is slow, certain, and planetary. It does not resolve by waiting. It does not have an acute phase followed by a survivable aftermath. Underground shelter provides no advantage against food system failure, atmospheric chemistry change, or a planet that is simply hotter for the next thousand years. The preparation pattern — blast doors, five-year food supplies, independent water and energy systems, staff quarters — is calibrated for months to years of isolation followed by return to surface. That is not a climate survival plan. It is an acute event survival plan.

The threats that fit that profile are nuclear exchange, supervolcanic eruption, major impact, and severe solar event. All share rapid onset, a finite catastrophic period, and a survivable aftermath if shelter holds. Underground preparation is coherent against all of them. It is not coherent against climate.

---

## What the Preparation Pattern Actually Shows

The documentation is extensive and comes from mainstream sources. Mark Zuckerberg is building a compound in Kauai, Hawaii, estimated at over $270 million, with a 5,000 square foot underground bunker equipped with blast-resistant doors, independent energy, water and food infrastructure, and an escape hatch. The property accommodates more than 100 people. Workers signed NDAs. Bill Gates reportedly has underground security areas beneath multiple homes. Peter Thiel attempted a bunker in New Zealand before local authorities rejected it. New Zealand appears repeatedly in this pattern — not as a random preference but as a destination that makes sense against a specific threat profile.

New Zealand sits outside the primary ashfall distribution zone for a Yellowstone supervolcanic eruption. It is in the southern hemisphere, where stratospheric particulate injection from a northern hemisphere eruption disperses more slowly. It has stable food production infrastructure, low population density, and geographic distance from the social collapse that would follow a northern hemisphere catastrophe. The Silicon Valley concentration of New Zealand interest is not casual. These are people with resources to go anywhere. They are choosing somewhere specific.

Nuclear exchange does not explain New Zealand. Most plausible nuclear scenarios leave New Zealand as dangerous as anywhere else within years of fallout and nuclear winter. The geographic pattern fits supervolcanic eruption better than any other candidate on the threat list.

---

## The 2025 Yellowstone Anomaly

Between July 2025 and January 2026, the north rim of Yellowstone Caldera experienced ground uplift at rates exceeding 15 centimeters per year. The USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory called this one of the fastest deformation rates ever recorded at Yellowstone. The official cause: unknown. The uplift stopped cleanly in January 2026.

This analysis downloaded the raw seismic catalog for that period directly from the USGS earthquake catalog search tool. Geographic bounds: latitude 44.0–45.2 North, longitude 111.5–109.5 West. Date range: July 1, 2025 through January 31, 2026. Minimum magnitude: 0.0. Both the University of Utah Seismograph Stations catalog and the USGS aggregate catalog were queried independently.

The numbers produced by direct analysis of 810 to 839 events are as follows.

Monthly event counts show a pronounced arc: July 51, August 93, September 81, October 172, November 242, December 76, January 95. The peak came in November — the month the USGS described as containing a swarm directly above the uplift center.

The November swarm produced 242 events. Zero of them occurred deeper than 15 kilometers. Every single event sat between 1.5 and 14.6 kilometers depth, with a mean of 5.86 kilometers. The spatial distribution held a stable centroid across all four weekly cluster windows at approximately 44.69 degrees North, 110.75 degrees West — within Norris Geyser Basin, the same location the USGS identified as the uplift center.

The depth ceiling is the finding that matters most. Natural magmatic activity moves through the full crustal column. Yellowstone's magma reservoir begins around 5 kilometers depth and extends to at least 10 kilometers, with a secondary reservoir reaching 46 kilometers. A magmatic or deep tectonic process would produce seismicity distributed through that full range. Instead, 242 events produced a hard ceiling at 15 kilometers. Nothing deeper. That ceiling is consistent with one specific mechanism: fluid injection into the hydrothermal system from above, where injected pressure propagates through the upper crust and stops where the injection-driven pressure change ends.

The broad spatial distribution — 67 kilometers latitude, 63 kilometers longitude — argues against a single injection point. A single wellhead produces a tight spatial cluster. Distributed multi-point injection produces exactly the diffuse pattern observed. Sophisticated infrastructure would not use a single point. A single point is immediately identifiable in the seismic record.

---

## The Missing Data

The University of Utah Seismograph Stations operates the Yellowstone Seismic Network. They are the primary data source for Yellowstone seismicity. Their public catalog is current through September 2024. Then it stops. The entire deformation period — July 2025 through January 2026 — is absent from their public record. This is not a general publication delay. The catalog was current up to September 2024 and then specifically absent for the anomalous window.

An inquiry was sent to UUSS asking about this absence. It has not been answered.

The data used in this analysis came from the USGS aggregate catalog independently of UUSS. The USGS data existed. The primary network's public record did not. That gap covers exactly the period that matters.

---

## The Infrastructure at the Centroid

The seismic centroid at 44.69 North, 110.75 West is Norris Geyser Basin. In August and September 2023 — twenty-two months before the deformation anomaly began — three organizations installed a new multi-component monitoring station at Ragged Hills, the center of Norris Geyser Basin. The installing organizations were the University of Utah, the USGS, and the EarthScope Consortium.

EarthScope Consortium was formed January 1, 2023, through the merger of the Incorporated Research Institutions for Seismology and UNAVCO. The Norris installation was among its first major field operations. The station included seismic sensors, a GPS station, an infrasound array, weather instrumentation, and borehole instruments.

Borehole instruments require drilling. A borehole housing monitoring equipment is physically identical to a borehole housing injection equipment. The distinction is in what gets installed. The specific equipment inside the boreholes beyond sensor designations is not detailed in public documentation.

EarthScope operates the Global Seismographic Network jointly with USGS. The GSN contributes directly to monitoring for nuclear explosions under the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. This is a defense-adjacent national security function, not peripheral to EarthScope's work but central to it.

The timeline: January 2023, EarthScope formed. August-September 2023, borehole infrastructure installed at Norris. July 2025, fastest recorded deformation event in Yellowstone's monitoring history begins at Norris. November 2025, seismic swarm directly above the uplift center, zero events below 15 kilometers. January 2026, deformation stops cleanly. UUSS public catalog absent for the entire anomalous period.

---

## The Institutional Timing

On November 20, 2025 — four months into the deformation event — the Department of Energy reorganized several offices. The Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management became the Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy Office, with geothermal operations added to its mandate.

In the FY2026 Energy and Water appropriations cycle — the budget period immediately following the deformation — the Senate Appropriations Committee called specifically for DOE to prioritize next-generation geothermal power production technologies, with up to $75 million including $40 million for demonstrations.

Each of these changes has an innocent explanation. Together, clustered around the specific period of the fastest recorded deformation at the world's most significant geothermal system, they form a pattern that warrants documentation.

---

## Chain of Reasoning to Findings

The chain runs as follows.

Ultra-wealthy individuals are building acute-event survival infrastructure at documented and accelerating scale. The geographic pattern of their relocation choices fits supervolcanic ashfall survivability mapping better than any other threat on the candidate list. Yellowstone experienced its fastest recorded deformation in monitoring history in 2025, cause officially unknown, with a seismic signature showing a hard depth ceiling consistent with hydrothermal injection from above. Borehole infrastructure capable of injection was installed at the deformation centroid twenty-two months before the anomaly began, by an organization with nuclear test ban treaty monitoring functions. The primary seismic network's public data is absent for the entire anomalous period. Institutional budget and organizational changes clustered around the deformation window.

None of these observations requires the others to exist. Each stands independently. Together they point in the same direction.

---

## Probability Assessment

The following conclusions are indexed by probability. These are not precise statistical estimates. They are honest assessments of where the evidence points, derived from the verified data above, with the verified data as the testing ground.

**Natural deformation event, all institutional timing coincidental — 25%**

The USGS characterization and the precedent of a similar 1996-2004 episode at the same location provide real support. Against this: the 2025 rate dramatically exceeded the prior episode, the hard 15-kilometer depth ceiling across 242 events is anomalous for natural magmatic or hydrothermal processes, the deformation stopped cleanly rather than declining gradually, and the UUSS data absence covers exactly the anomalous window rather than reflecting general publication delays.

**Natural escalating trend privately known to institutions, driving preparation without active intervention — 15%**

The long-term seismic intensification at Yellowstone documented across 1984-2025 is real and documented. Institutions with access to non-public monitoring data could have concluded that Yellowstone is on a natural trajectory toward eventual eruption on a timescale of decades, and prepared accordingly without actively accelerating anything. This conclusion does not require the 2025 deformation to be managed. It requires only that the preparation pattern reflects private knowledge of a natural trajectory.

**Managed subsurface fluid injection as capability test and deployment preparation — 55%**

Physical borehole infrastructure confirmed at the deformation centroid. Defense-adjacent organization confirmed as installer. Hard depth ceiling consistent with hydrothermal injection from above. Clean cessation consistent with controlled termination. UUSS data absent for exact period. Budget and organizational changes clustered around the deformation window. The geographic preparation pattern consistent with known future event rather than merely anticipated risk.

This conclusion merges what might be called the test phase and the deployment phase because they are not separate conclusions. Testing a system and intending to deploy it are sequential phases of the same operation. A capability test validates the mechanism, characterizes the response, and confirms the methodology. The 2025 episode, if managed, did exactly that: it produced six months of controlled deformation, characterized the seismic response, confirmed the depth ceiling of the affected zone, and terminated cleanly. That is what a test looks like.

**Coincidental institutional timing with no operational connection — 5%**

The UUSS data absence being specific to the anomalous period rather than reflecting a general publication delay is near-decisive against pure coincidence. Multiple independent coincidences — formation of EarthScope, borehole installation, deformation onset, budget reorganization, geothermal funding — clustering into the same eighteen-month window approaches statistical impossibility under a null hypothesis of independence.

---

## What Would Change These Numbers

Evidence that would move probability toward natural explanation: UUSS releasing the 2025-2026 seismic catalog showing data existed and was simply delayed, independent geological analysis finding the depth ceiling consistent with a specific natural hydrothermal mechanism, or EarthScope releasing equipment manifests showing no injection capability in the Norris boreholes.

Evidence that would move probability toward managed injection: procurement records for the Norris borehole installation showing equipment beyond standard monitoring sensors, any indication that the UUSS data absence was directed rather than technical, additional deformation episodes at Norris following the same pattern, or corroborating evidence of operational planning connecting the preparation infrastructure to Yellowstone specifically.

The investigation reached the limit of what public records can currently provide. The next steps require either institutional response, Freedom of Information requests targeting the Norris installation equipment manifests and the UUSS data gap, or independent geological analysis of the November 2025 swarm spatial distribution by researchers outside the USGS-EarthScope-UUSS network.

---

## What This Means

If the 55% conclusion is correct, a capability test was conducted at Yellowstone in 2025. The test validated that subsurface fluid injection through existing borehole infrastructure at Norris Geyser Basin produces measurable ground deformation confined to the upper 15 kilometers of crust, distributed across a 60-kilometer radius, reversible by terminating injection, and detectable primarily through the monitoring network whose public data then went dark for the duration.

The people preparing underground facilities in New Zealand and Hawaii are not preparing for something they fear might happen. They are preparing for something they know is planned.

That is a specific and serious claim. The evidence does not prove it. It supports it at 55% probability against alternatives that collectively account for 45%. In any rational risk framework, a 55% probability of deliberate institutional preparation for a manufactured supervolcanic event warrants investigation at a level that has not yet occurred publicly.

This paper is one step toward that investigation. The data is public. The catalog is downloadable. The borehole installation is documented. The budget records are available. Anyone with geological training and access to the raw seismic data can replicate this analysis and extend it.

The question is not whether the data exists. The question is whether anyone will look at it.

---

*This analysis was produced through direct examination of publicly available data sources including the USGS Earthquake Catalog, NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory atmospheric records, Congressional appropriations documents, and published geological literature. All probability assessments represent honest evaluation of documented evidence and should be treated as hypothesis-level conclusions requiring further investigation rather than established findings.*
